p: The Greek has "among those who press her"; the Hebrew has "between the narrow places".

readings.en: between the narrow places
readings.plain: in the narrow places

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: among those who press her
readings.plain: among her oppressors

why: The Hebrew consonants can be read either way, and "narrow places" is the Masoretic reading and fits the picture of a cornered fugitive (Psalm 118:5). The Greek is a translation, not a different Hebrew text. 4Q111 preserves this verse, but in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription the word "the narrow places" is restored, so the scroll gives no help.

a: Jerusalem remembers her days of misery and homelessness, all the treasures she had in ancient days.
p: 4Q111 seems to read "Remember, LORD, all our pains", turning the sentence into a prayer.

readings.orig: זָכְרָה יְרוּשָׁלִַם יְמֵי עָנְיָהּ וּמְרוּדֶיהָ כֹּל מַחֲמֻדֶּיהָ אֲשֶׁר הָיוּ מִימֵי קֶדֶם
readings.en: Jerusalem remembers the days of her affliction and wandering, all her precious things from days of old
readings.plain: Jerusalem remembers her days of misery and homelessness, all the treasures she had in ancient days.

readings.w: 4Q111 (4QLam, a Qumran scroll), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook; damaged
readings.orig: זכורה יהוה [כול] מכאובנו אשר היו מימי קדם
readings.en: Remember, LORD, [all] our pains that have been from days of old (the word in brackets is restored)
readings.plain: Remember, LORD, all our pains, which have been ours since ancient days.

why: The Masoretic Text is the base and makes a smooth sentence. In the transcription 4Q111 has the divine name where the Masoretic Text has "Jerusalem", and "our pains" where it has "the days of her affliction and wandering ... precious things"; "all" is restored. The scroll also lacks "she looks" (ra'uhah) in the last line and reads "her adversaries" (sareha) where the Masoretic Text has tsarim, "foes". It is one witness, partly broken, so it is shown as a possibility, not followed.
b: Only 4Q111 preserves this verse among the scrolls. The same scroll differs from the Masoretic Text at the end of the verse too (see the next entry).

t: Her ruin, her Sabbaths, or her dwelling?
p: The rare Hebrew word was read four ways in antiquity.

readings.en: at her ending / ruin (mishbatehah)
readings.plain: they laughed at her ruin

readings.en: at [all] her breakings (the word in brackets is restored)
readings.plain: they laughed at her breaking

readings.en: her Sabbaths (reading the Hebrew as shabbatot)
readings.plain: they laughed at her Sabbaths

readings.en: over her dwelling (a form like moshavah)
readings.plain: they laughed over her dwelling place

why: Mishbat occurs only here. The Masoretic reading, from the root "to stop", gives "ruin", which fits the mocking of defeat; 4Q111's "breakings" comes to nearly the same sense. "Sabbaths" is a possible reading (Lamentations 2:6) but is a single ancient witness.

a: Does this not concern you, you travelers on the road?
p: The Greek and Latin have no "not"; the Hebrew has it, as 4Q111 does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008), with 4Q111
readings.en: Not to you, all you who pass by on the road?
readings.plain: Does this not concern you, you travelers on the road?

readings.w: Greek (Swete, Codex Vaticanus) and Jerome's Vulgate
readings.orig: Οἱ πρὸς ὑμᾶς πάντες παραπορευόμενοι ὁδόν; "o vos omnes qui transitis per viam"
readings.en: O all you who pass by on the road
readings.plain: O all you travelers on the road!

why: The Masoretic Text and 4Q111 agree (the scroll writes the word lo). The Greek and Latin may have read a different Hebrew word (lu, "if only", or the same letters read as a call) or taken the negative as an exclamation. The Hebrew is hard, but there is no Hebrew witness for dropping it. The scroll also reads hogirani (as transcribed) where the Masoretic Text has hugah, "he made [me] grieve"; the scroll's form is a different verb, and the Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

t: Fire that conquered, or fire brought down?
p: The Greek takes the verb as "come down" and not "rule".

readings.en: and it ruled / overpowered them
readings.plain: and it conquered them

readings.en: he brought it down
readings.plain: and he brought it down

why: The Masoretic form, from radah, is well attested for dominating (Leviticus 26:17). The Greek could come from yarad ("come down"), but the Hebrew reading makes sense, and the Greek is one witness.

p: The rare Hebrew verb is "was bound" or "was watchful"; 4Q111 has the plainer "was tied".

readings.en: was bound (a rare verb; or 'was watched')
readings.plain: is bound on

readings.en: was tied on
readings.plain: is tied on

why: The Masoretic verb occurs only here. The Greek (Swete) reads "he watched over my rebellions", taking it as the verb "to watch" (shaqad). 4Q111 reads niqshera, "was tied", a different verb of similar sound and meaning. The scroll also reads the divine name YHWH where the Masoretic Text has Adonay at the end of the verse. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text, whose sense the scroll supports.

a: my eye, my eye runs down with water
p: The Hebrew says "my eye, my eye"; the Greek has one and 4Q111 has a different wording.

readings.en: my eye, my eye runs down water
readings.plain: my eye, my eye runs down with water

readings.en: my eyes wept, my tears ran down
readings.plain: my eye runs down with my tears

readings.en: my eye brought down water
readings.plain: my eye runs down with water

why: The doubling is the harder reading, and a copyist would be more likely to drop one "eye" than add one. 4Q111 differs in other words too, so it is a different text of the verse, not only a copying slip.

a: there is no one to comfort her
p: The scroll 4Q111 has extra words in 1:17, including "you are righteous, LORD".

readings.orig: אֵין מְנַחֵם לָהּ צִוָּה יְהוָה לְיַעֲקֹב סְבִיבָיו צָרָיו ... צַדִּיק הוּא יְהוָה
readings.en: no one to comfort her. The LORD ordered ... Jacob's neighbors his foes ... The LORD is righteous
readings.plain: there is no one to comfort her

readings.w: 4Q111 (4QLam, a Qumran scroll), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook; damaged
readings.orig: אין מנחם לה מכול אוהביה צדיק אתה יהוה צפה אדוני ליעקוב ... צדיק הוא [אדוני]
readings.en: no one to comfort her from all her lovers; you are righteous, LORD; [a verb written tsafah] the Lord ... for Jacob ... righteous is he, [the Lord, restored]
readings.plain: there is no one to comfort her from all her lovers; you are righteous, LORD

why: Several words are visible in the scroll: "from all her lovers", "you are righteous", "LORD" and "the Lord" after a verb written tsafah, where the Masoretic Text has tsivvah, "ordered". In 1:17 the scroll also has "Zion" where the Masoretic Text has "Jerusalem". At 1:18 the scroll preserves only "righteous is he"; its Adonay is restored, so it is not counted as the scroll's reading. The plus puts a confession addressed to God ("you are righteous") into 1:17, where 1:18 has it in the third person. It may be an intrusion of the confession of 1:18, or may reflect a different arrangement of the verses; no view is settled. One damaged witness is not enough to change the base text, so the Plain follows the Masoretic Text.
b: Only 4Q111 preserves 1:17-18. The pe verse (1:17) and tsade verse (1:18) of the alphabet are both in the scroll, in this form.

a: wrecked his shelter like a garden hut
t: Like a garden, or like a vine?
p: The Greek reads "like a vine", which Job 15:33 supports.

readings.en: he treated violently, like a garden, his booth
readings.plain: wrecked his shelter like a garden hut

readings.orig: διεπέτασεν ὡς ἄμπελον τὸ σκήνωμα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: he spread out his tent like a vine
readings.plain: stripped his shelter like a vine

why: The Hebrew kaggan "like a garden" is the base. Job 15:33 uses the same verb (chamas) of a vine that is stripped of its grapes, which suggests a vine here (kegefen); the Greek may reflect that. Because the Masoretic reading also gives a sensible picture (a flimsy garden hut, Isaiah 1:8), the Plain keeps it.
b: The Greek also takes mo'ed as "his festival" in the next phrase, not "the place where he meets his people".

a: Your ruin is as big as the sea
t: A sea of ruin, or a cup?
p: The Greek reads "the cup of your ruin has grown great".

readings.en: great as the sea is your breaking
readings.plain: Your ruin is as big as the sea

readings.en: the cup of your ruin has grown great
readings.plain: The cup of your ruin has grown big

why: The Hebrew "as the sea" is a clear comparison (compare Jeremiah 6:14). The Greek has a different sense, the cup of wrath (4:21), but no Hebrew witness has it.

a: we have not come to our end
t: "We are not finished" or "they are not finished"?
p: The Hebrew verb is first person plural; the Greek manuscripts that supply the verse, the Peshitta, the Targum and some Hebrew manuscripts have a third person.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); Jerome's Vulgate ("we are not consumed")
readings.en: that we have not come to an end (tamnu)
readings.plain: we have not come to our end

readings.w: Greek (the manuscripts that supply the verse: Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus), the Peshitta, the Targum and some Hebrew manuscripts, as reported by Albrektson
readings.en: that they (his acts of loyal love) have not come to an end (tammu)
readings.plain: they have not come to an end

why: This is not a conjecture: the third-person reading has several versions and some Hebrew manuscripts behind it, and it fits the next line, whose subject is "his compassions". The Masoretic Text, with the Vulgate, makes sense too if "we" is read as a result: because of the LORD's acts of loyal love we have not been finished off. Because the versions could have smoothed the verb to match the next line, and the Masoretic reading is acceptable, the Plain follows the base text; the witnesses are split. Codex Vaticanus, as Swete prints it, has no text at 3:22-24 or at 3:29 (it omits them), so the Greek of these verses is not read from it. The Targum and Peshitta are not among the witnesses read for this site; they are named here as reported. No Qumran scroll preserves this verse.

p: The written form is tanin; the form read aloud is tannim, "jackals".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008), as read aloud (Qere)
readings.en: jackals (tannim)
readings.plain: Even jackals

readings.w: The written form (Ketiv) תנין, which the Greek ("dragons") and the Vulgate ("lamiae") understood as a monster or serpent
readings.en: a sea monster or serpent (tannin)
readings.plain: Even sea monsters

why: Mothers nursing their young is a fact about animals; jackals suckle their pups, and sea monsters are unlikely to be pictured doing it (compare Micah 1:8 and Job 30:29, where jackals and ostriches go together). The Plain follows the Qere. The verse has a second Ketiv/Qere, written ki ("for"), read ka- ("like") before "ostriches", which does not change the sense.

t: The LORD's anointed, or "Christ the Lord"?
p: The Greek and Latin put the two words side by side: "Christ [the] Lord".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); 5Q6 and 5Q7 preserve the divine name
readings.en: the LORD's anointed
readings.plain: the LORD's anointed

readings.en: Christ [the] Lord
readings.plain: the anointed Lord

why: The Hebrew genitive is the same phrase used of Saul and David (1 Samuel 24:6). The Greek and Latin are translations that set the two words in apposition; they do not have a different Hebrew text. Both Qumran scrolls that preserve the verse show the divine name after the word "anointed" (the word "anointed" is restored in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription, not visible).

p: Codex Vaticanus has "the chosen men took up weeping".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); 5Q6 preserves the verse
readings.en: young men lift a mill
readings.plain: Young men carry the millstone

readings.en: chosen men took up weeping
readings.plain: The chosen men took up weeping

why: 5Q6 preserves 5:13 and agrees with the Masoretic words as far as they are not restored. The Greek reads the Hebrew differently (probably bachurim as "chosen" and the next word as "weeping"), and it is one witness.

a: unless you have rejected us altogether
p: The Greek and Latin take the last verse as a statement, not an "unless".

readings.en: unless you have utterly rejected us (or: but you have utterly rejected us)
readings.plain: unless you have rejected us altogether

readings.w: Greek (Swete) "for you have utterly rejected us"; Vulgate "but throwing us away you have rejected us"
readings.orig: ὅτι ἀπωθούμενος ἀπώσω ἡμᾶς; sed proiciens reppulisti nos
readings.en: for you have rejected us altogether
readings.plain: for you have rejected us altogether

why: The Hebrew particles ki 'im can mean "unless" or "but". All the Hebrew is the same; the question is how to read it. No scroll preserves 5:19-22. The Plain keeps "unless", which leaves the verse as an uncertainty and not a verdict; the Greek and Latin turn it into a statement. See the note at 5:22.
